problemTypes.title: Segment-table translation and limit checks
recipe: Look up the base and limit for the segment number.
Trap if offset ≥ limit; otherwise physical address = base + offset.
In segmented paging, split the offset further into a page number and a page offset and index that segment's page table.
problemTypes.trap: Accepting an offset equal to the limit, or adding the offset to the limit instead of the base.

problemTypes.title: Belady's anomaly and stack-algorithm properties
recipe: Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT, and any policy whose ranking of pages does not depend on the frame count) never fault more with more frames.
FIFO and second chance are not stack algorithms and can show the anomaly.
To demonstrate it, run FIFO with 3 and 4 frames on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: 9 faults against 10.
problemTypes.trap: Calling the anomaly FIFO-only, or reading it as proof that FIFO is always worse than LRU.

problemTypes.title: Page faults of a nested loop over a two-dimensional array
recipe: Find elements per page P ÷ b and bytes per row C × b; C stores arrays row-major, so A[i][j] lives at offset (i × C + j) × b.
Row-wise loop (i outer, j inner): consecutive accesses share a page, so faults = number of pages the array spans, ⌈R·C·b ÷ P⌉.

Column-wise loop (j outer, i inner): consecutive accesses jump C × b bytes. If a row fills at least a page and fewer than R frames are available, every access lands on a page evicted since its last use: R × C faults.
If two or more rows share a page, a column pass touches only ⌈R·C·b ÷ P⌉ pages; check whether those all fit in the frames before calling every access a fault.
problemTypes.trap: Counting the row-wise figure for a column-wise loop, or forgetting that the frame count decides whether the column pass keeps its pages.

problemTypes.title: Working set and working-set size at a given time
recipe: Number the references from 1; the working set at time t with window Δ is the set of distinct pages among references t − Δ + 1 to t.
Count the distinct pages: that is WSS(t, Δ). Include reference t itself.
For thrashing questions, add the working-set sizes of all processes and compare the sum with the available frames.
problemTypes.trap: Taking the window one reference off (references t − Δ to t − 1), or counting repeated pages more than once.

questions.stem: A process has 3 page frames, initially empty, and uses LRU replacement. How many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5? Count the faults that fill the empty frames too.
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 are compulsory faults. 4 evicts 1, the least recently used, leaving 2 3 4; 1 evicts 2 (3 4 1); 2 evicts 3 (4 1 2); 5 evicts 4 (1 2 5). Then 1 and 2 hit. 3 evicts 5, whose last use is older than those of 1 and 2 (1 2 3); 4 evicts 1 (2 3 4); 5 evicts 2 (3 4 5). Faults: 3 + 7 = 10.

questions.stem: For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with 3 initially empty frames, how many page faults does the Optimal (OPT) replacement policy cause?
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 are compulsory faults. 4 evicts 3, whose next use (the 10th reference) is farthest away, leaving 1 2 4. 1 and 2 hit. 5 evicts 4, next used at the 11th reference, after 1 and 2 (1 2 5). 1 and 2 hit. 3 evicts 1 or 2, neither of which is used again; 4 then evicts either page other than 5, since neither is used again. 5 hits. Faults: 3 + 4 = 7. 6 is OPT's count with 4 frames, and 9 and 10 are FIFO's and LRU's counts with 3 frames.

questions.stem: Under FIFO replacement with initially empty frames, how many page faults does the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 cause with 3 frames and with 4 frames, respectively?
questions.explanation: 3 frames: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5 all fault (4 evicts 1, 1 evicts 2, 2 evicts 3, 5 evicts 4), 1 and 2 hit, 3 evicts 1, 4 evicts 2 and 5 hits: 9 faults. 4 frames: 1 to 4 fault, 1 and 2 hit, and then 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 each evict the oldest page and all fault: 10 faults. More frames, more faults: Belady's anomaly. 10 and 8 are LRU's counts and 7 and 6 are OPT's.

questions.stem: Which of these page-replacement policies can cause more page faults when a process is given more frames (Belady's anomaly)?
questions.explanation: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: the pages resident with n frames are always a subset of those resident with n + 1 frames, so extra frames never add a fault. FIFO is the classic counterexample, with 9 faults on 3 frames and 10 on 4 for 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Second chance is not a stack algorithm either: when each newly loaded page gets reference bit 1, it makes exactly FIFO's choices on that string and also faults 9 times with 3 frames and 10 times with 4. If new pages get bit 0 instead, the string 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3 faults 4 times with 2 frames and 5 times with 3, so clock can show the anomaly under either convention.

questions.stem: A machine has 32-bit virtual addresses, 36-bit physical addresses and 8 KB pages (1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes). Each page-table entry holds the frame number plus 4 control bits, rounded up to a whole number of bytes. What is the size of one process's single-level page table?
questions.explanation: The offset is log₂ 8192 = 13 bits, so the VPN has 32 − 13 = 19 bits and the table has 2¹⁹ entries. The frame number has 36 − 13 = 23 bits; with 4 control bits an entry needs 27 bits, rounded up to 4 bytes. Size = 2¹⁹ × 4 B = 2²¹ B = 2 MB. 1.6875 MB skips the rounding, 4 MB assumes 4 KB pages and 32 MB counts one entry per physical frame.

questions.stem: Virtual addresses are 46 bits, pages are 8 KB (1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes) and every page-table entry is 4 bytes. If each table at every level must fit in exactly one page, how many levels does the hierarchical page table need?
questions.explanation: The offset is 13 bits, so the VPN has 46 − 13 = 33 bits. One page holds 8 KB ÷ 4 B = 2¹¹ entries, so each level resolves 11 bits, and 33 ÷ 11 = 3 levels; the outermost table is exactly 2¹¹ × 4 B = 8 KB, one page. Taking 4 KB pages by mistake gives 34 VPN bits at 10 bits per level, hence the wrong answer 4.

questions.stem: A 32-bit machine uses 4 KB pages, 4-byte page-table entries and a two-level page table split 10 + 10 + 12. Every table occupies one page, and an inner table exists only if some page it maps is in use. A process uses only the lowest 8 MB of its address space (code and data) and the highest 4 MB (stack). How many KB do its page tables occupy in total? (1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes, 1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes)
questions.explanation: An inner table has 2¹⁰ entries, each mapping a 4 KB page, so it covers 2¹⁰ × 4 KB = 4 MB. The lowest 8 MB needs the inner tables for outer entries 0 and 1, and the highest 4 MB needs the one for entry 1023: 3 inner tables. Adding the outer table gives 4 tables × 4 KB = 16 KB, against 2²⁰ × 4 B = 4 MB for a single-level table.

questions.stem: A paging system keeps a single-level page table in memory. A TLB lookup takes 5 ns, a memory access takes 100 ns and the TLB hit ratio is 0.96. The TLB is searched before every memory reference, so its lookup time is paid on hits and on misses. Ignoring page faults, what is the effective memory-access time in ns?
questions.explanation: A hit costs the lookup plus the data access: 5 + 100 = 105 ns. A miss costs the lookup, one access to read the page-table entry and the data access: 5 + 100 + 100 = 205 ns. EAT = 0.96 × 105 + 0.04 × 205 = 100.8 + 8.2 = 109 ns.

questions.stem: Memory access takes 100 ns. Servicing a page fault takes 8 ms when the victim page is clean (or a free frame exists) and 20 ms when the victim is dirty and must first be written back; 70% of victims are dirty. One access in 10⁶ causes a page fault. Using EAT = (1 − p) × memory time + p × fault-service time, what is the effective access time in ns? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Average service time s = 0.3 × 8 + 0.7 × 20 = 16.4 ms = 1.64 × 10⁷ ns. With p = 10⁻⁶, EAT = (1 − 10⁻⁶) × 100 + 10⁻⁶ × 1.64 × 10⁷ = 99.9999 + 16.4 ≈ 116.4 ns. A fault rate of one in a million already makes memory about 16% slower.

questions.stem: A segment table holds (base, limit) = (2000, 500) for segment 0, (3100, 120) for segment 1, (700, 900) for segment 2 and (5200, 300) for segment 3. Which logical address (segment, offset) is translated without a trap, and to which physical address?
questions.explanation: A reference is legal only if offset < limit. (1, 120) fails because 120 is not below 120, (3, 310) fails because 310 ≥ 300 and (0, 512) fails because 512 ≥ 500. Only (2, 850) passes (850 < 900), giving 700 + 850 = 1550. The other three addresses are what base + offset would give without the limit check.

questions.stem: Which of the following memory-management schemes suffer from external fragmentation?
questions.explanation: External fragmentation arises when variable-sized blocks are carved out of memory: segments and variable partitions leave holes between them that may be too small for the next request. Paging uses equal-sized frames, so any free frame fits any page and only the last page of a process wastes space (internal fragmentation). Segmented paging stores every segment in pages, so it too has only internal fragmentation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about page tables and the TLB are true?
options: An inverted page table has one entry per physical frame, so its number of entries does not depend on the virtual address space.
A two-level page table never occupies more memory than a single-level table for the same address space.
A TLB miss on a page that is in memory is resolved by a page-table walk, with no disk access.
The number of entries in a single-level page table is fixed by the size of physical memory.
questions.explanation: The inverted table is indexed by frame, and a TLB miss is not a page fault, so those two statements hold. The two-level claim fails when the whole address space is in use: every inner table is needed plus the outer table, so the hierarchy is slightly larger than the flat table. The physical-memory claim mixes up the two widths: a conventional table has one entry per virtual page, so the virtual address width sets the number of entries, while the physical address width sets the size of each entry.

questions.stem: Free holes in address order are 150, 200, 350, 500 and 550 KB. Requests of 530, 240, 350 and 250 KB arrive in that order, and each allocation leaves the unused part of its hole as a smaller hole. Which placement policy satisfies all four requests?
questions.explanation: Every policy must put 530 KB in the 550 KB hole (20 KB left). First fit and best fit then both place 240 KB in the 350 KB hole (110 left) and 350 KB in the 500 KB hole (150 left); next fit, searching on from the 550 KB hole, wraps around and makes the same two choices. All three are left with holes of 150, 200, 110, 150 and 20 KB, so 250 KB fails. Worst fit puts 240 KB in the 500 KB hole (260 left), fills the 350 KB hole exactly with the 350 KB request and fits 250 KB into the 260 KB remainder.

questions.stem: Four frames hold pages A, B, C and D in clock order, with reference bits 1, 1, 0 and 1, and the clock hand points at A. On a fault the hand clears each set bit it passes and advances; it replaces the first page whose bit is already 0, gives the new page reference bit 1 and moves one frame past it. Two faults occur with no hits in between, loading E and then F. Which pages are evicted?
questions.explanation: First fault: A and B have bit 1, so both are cleared and skipped; C has bit 0 and is replaced by E (bit 1), and the hand moves to D. Second fault: D's bit is cleared and the hand moves on to A, whose bit was cleared during the first sweep, so A is replaced by F. Evicting D second ignores its reference bit, and A then B is plain FIFO from the hand.

questions.stem: CPU utilisation has collapsed and the paging disk is saturated because the combined working sets of the running processes exceed physical memory. Which action restores throughput?
options: Admit more processes so the CPU has more work to do
Suspend some processes until the remaining working sets fit in memory
Shorten the CPU time quantum so processes take turns faster
Switch page replacement from LRU to FIFO
questions.explanation: The system is thrashing: the total working-set demand exceeds the available frames, so every process keeps faulting. Swapping some processes out frees their frames, and each remaining process can then hold its working set. Admitting more processes, the reflex of a scheduler that sees an idle CPU, deepens the shortage; a shorter quantum or a different replacement policy creates no frames.

questions.stem: Fifty free frames are shared by three processes of 20, 45 and 135 pages using proportional allocation, with each share rounded down and any leftover frame kept in the free pool. How many frames does each process receive?
questions.explanation: The total size is 20 + 45 + 135 = 200 pages, so the shares are 50 × 20/200 = 5, 50 × 45/200 = 11.25 and 50 × 135/200 = 33.75. Rounding down gives 5, 11 and 33, leaving 1 frame free. 5, 11 and 34 rounds to the nearest instead, 5, 12 and 34 rounds up and would need 51 frames, and 16 each is equal allocation.

questions.stem: A machine has 16-bit virtual addresses and 1 KB pages (1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes). The page table maps virtual page 10 to physical frame 5. What physical address does virtual address 0x2A5C translate to?
questions.explanation: The offset is log₂ 1024 = 10 bits, leaving 6 VPN bits. 0x2A5C = 0010 1010 0101 1100₂: the top six bits 001010₂ give VPN 10 and the low ten bits 10 0101 1100₂ = 0x25C give the offset. Frame 5 starts at 5 × 1024 = 0x1400, so the physical address is 0x1400 + 0x25C = 0x165C. 0x525C writes the frame's hex digit in front of the offset's hex digits, which works only when the offset is a whole number of hex digits; 0x145C drops the offset's top bit; 0x0A5C keeps the low 12 bits of the virtual address.

questions.stem: A paging system has a single-level page table in memory and a TLB that is searched before every reference. A TLB lookup takes 10 ns, a memory access 100 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 0.9. Of all memory references, 0.01% cause a page fault (a fault is detected only after the page-table entry is read on a TLB miss), and servicing a fault, including the restarted access, takes 5 ms. What is the effective memory-access time in ns, rounded to the nearest integer?
questions.explanation: Three paths. TLB hit (0.9): 10 + 100 = 110 ns. TLB miss, page resident (1 − 0.9 − 0.0001 = 0.0999): 10 + 100 + 100 = 210 ns. Page fault (0.0001): 10 + 100 + 5 × 10⁶ ns. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.0999 × 210 + 0.0001 × 5,000,110 = 99 + 20.979 + 500.011 = 619.99 ≈ 620 ns. One fault in ten thousand references costs more than four times the rest of the access time combined; leaving s in milliseconds would give about 120 ns.

questions.stem: An array int A[512][512] with 4-byte ints is stored in row-major order starting on a page boundary. Pages are 2 KB (1 KB = 2¹⁰ bytes), the array gets 128 page frames that are initially empty, replacement is LRU, and the code and loop variables live elsewhere. How many page faults does the loop for (j = 0; j < 512; j++) for (i = 0; i < 512; i++) A[i][j] = 0; cause on A?
questions.explanation: A row holds 512 × 4 = 2048 bytes, exactly one page, so row i is page i. The inner loop walks down a column and touches pages 0, 1, …, 511 in turn. With 128 frames LRU keeps only the 128 most recent rows, so when the next column starts at row 0, that page was evicted 384 references earlier. Every access faults: 512 × 512 = 262,144. Swapping the loops (i outer) would fault only once per page, 512 times, and so would this loop with 512 or more frames.

questions.stem: A process makes the page references 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 4, 5, 4, 4, 5, 6, 5, 6, 6, 7, 1, numbered 1 to 16. The working set at time t with window Δ is the set of distinct pages among the Δ most recent references up to and including reference t. With Δ = 5, what is the working-set size at t = 16?
questions.explanation: The window is references 12 to 16: 5, 6, 6, 7, 1. The distinct pages are {5, 6, 7, 1}, so the size is 4. Shifting the window back one reference (11 to 15: 6, 5, 6, 6, 7) gives 3, the usual off-by-one slip. At t = 10 the window 4, 5, 4, 4, 5 gives only 2, which shows the working set shrinking inside a locality and growing at a transition.

questions.stem: A process calls fork() on a system that implements copy-on-write. Which of the following statements are true?
options: Right after the fork, parent and child map the same physical frames, with the shared pages marked read-only.
When either process first writes to a shared page, a fault occurs and the OS copies only that page.
The fork copies the parent's whole address space into new frames before the child runs.
A page that neither process ever writes is read in again from disk for the child.
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write defers copying: the child's page table points at the parent's frames, and both mappings are made read-only. A write traps as a protection fault; the handler copies that one page, maps the copy writable and restarts the write. Copying everything at fork time is exactly what copy-on-write avoids, and a page that is never written stays shared in its existing frame with no disk access at all.

pitfalls.text: Paging removes external fragmentation, not internal: the last page of each process is on average half empty, and larger pages waste more.
A TLB miss is not a page fault. The page may be resident; the miss adds only a page-table walk, with no disk access.
Say whether the TLB lookup time is charged on a miss: serial and overlapped lookups give different EATs, and a k-level table adds k memory accesses on a miss, not one.
Belady's anomaly is not FIFO-only: second chance can show it too. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT are immune.
Count compulsory faults: with empty frames the first reference to every distinct page is a fault and belongs in the total, unless the question asks only for replacements.
Effective access time mixes nanoseconds and milliseconds. Convert the fault-service time (1 ms = 10⁶ ns) before multiplying by the fault rate.
The virtual address width sets how many page-table entries there are; the physical address width sets how wide each entry is. Swapping them is the classic slip.
A segment offset is legal only if it is strictly less than the limit; an offset equal to the limit traps.

revisionCard.heading: Allocation
lines: First fit: first hole that fits (fastest); best fit: smallest that fits; worst fit: largest
Fixed partitions → internal fragmentation; variable partitions → external
Compaction cures external fragmentation but copies memory
Paging: internal fragmentation only; segmentation brings external back
Segmented paging: every segment paged, no external fragmentation

revisionCard.heading: Paging and TLB
lines: Offset d = log₂(page size); VPN = v − d bits; PFN = p − d bits
Single-level table = 2^VPN × entry size (32-bit, 4 KB, 4 B → 4 MB)
Inverted table: one entry per frame, looked up by hashing (pid, VPN)
EAT = t + h·m + (1 − h)(m_PT + m); single level: m_PT = m
TLB miss ≠ page fault

revisionCard.heading: Virtual memory
lines: EAT = (1 − p)·m + p·s, with s converted to ns
FIFO: Belady's anomaly; OPT: fewest faults, needs the future; LRU: practical; clock approximates LRU
Thrashing: working sets exceed memory → reduce multiprogramming; PFF tunes frames per process

lines: Levels = ⌈VPN bits ÷ log₂(page size ÷ entry size)⌉
k-level table: a TLB miss costs (k + 1) memory accesses
Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT) never show Belady's anomaly; FIFO and clock can
Same string with FIFO: 9 faults on 3 frames, 10 on 4

errata.correction: Second chance (clock) shows it too. When each newly loaded page gets reference bit 1, clock makes FIFO's choices on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and faults 9 times with 3 frames but 10 times with 4; with new pages given bit 0, the string 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3 faults 4 times with 2 frames but 5 times with 3. LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never show it.

errata.claim: PYQ-9: "Min frames to avoid Belady's? A: LRU avoids it."
errata.correction: The answer names a policy instead of a frame count, and no frame count would be right: for every n ≥ 3 some reference string makes FIFO fault more with n + 1 frames than with n (the classic string scales up as 1…n+1, 1…n−1, n+2, 1…n+2). Only the choice of policy avoids the anomaly; stack algorithms such as LRU and Optimal never fault more when frames are added.

errata.claim: TLB shootdown: on a VM update or context switch, invalidate stale entries.
errata.correction: A TLB shootdown is the cross-processor invalidation done when a mapping changes on a multiprocessor: the CPU that changed the page table interrupts the others so they drop the stale entry. Discarding entries on a context switch is an ordinary TLB flush, which address-space identifiers (ASIDs) make unnecessary.
